description:
Équipe de 4 passionnés par les sciences terrestres et le changement climatique. Nous combinons développement, design et data analysis pour transformer des données NASA en solutions accessibles. Compétences 

complémentaires, motivation forte. Prêts pour Earth System Trend Detective!
summary: Pluie Prévue is a web tool that explores whether ocean signals can help anticipate monthly rainfall in the Sahel and West Africa. We combine more than 40 years of CHIRPS satellite rainfall with El Niño (ONI) and Atlantic sea-surface temperature signals, and train an XGBoost model that forecasts rainfall anomalies 1 and 3 months ahead. The interface offers an interactive rainfall map, anomaly layers (deficit / normal / surplus), time series for cities such as Dakar, Niamey and Ouagadougou, ocean-signal charts, and a plain-language assistant. Our main result is deliberately honest: on a chronological test, the model does not beat the monthly climatology (skill -0.40 at 1 month, -0.49 at 3 months). We report this as a valid negative result, show every forecast next to its climatological baseline with a p10-p90 range, and state clearly that this is an experimental statistical tool, not an operational warning. It matters because farmers, energy planners and educators in the Sahel need transparent, uncertainty-aware information.
details:
What it does: Pluie Prévue forecasts rainfall anomalies (difference from the normal of the same calendar month) 1 and 3 months ahead over West Africa and the Sahel, and shows them with their uncertainty and with a baseline forecast (the monthly climatology).

How it works: Monthly rainfall comes from CHIRPS v3.0 (1981 onward). Predictors are the El Niño index (ONI) and Atlantic sea-surface temperature, with lags of a few months. An XGBoost model is trained on the early period and evaluated on a later, chronological test period with no random shuffling. A FastAPI backend serves the 1-month and 3-month models; a web front end displays the map, anomaly layers, city time series, ocean signals, model comparison and a "limits" page. Each forecast is shown with a p10-p90 range.

Results (honest): the model does not beat the climatology on our test (skill vs climatology: -0.40 at 1 month, -0.49 at 3 months). We kept our evaluation rules fixed before computing results and publish the negative result as is. This is consistent with the literature: ocean signals explain only part of Sahel rainfall variability, and we have few years of data.

Benefits and intended impact: a transparent, educational tool for agriculture (anticipating deficits), energy (coupling with solar forecasts) and research/teaching on ENSO-Sahel links. The tool always shows performance metrics and limits.

Limits: experimental statistical tool, not an operational alert; no storm-scale prediction;

correlation is not causation; satellite rainfall has errors, larger in the north; few years of data, so apparent links can be due to chance. The free-tier API may need a few seconds to wake up on first call. Tools: Python (pandas , AirFlow, XGBoost), FastAPI (FastAPI Cloud), web front end on Vercel, interactive map layer.

Creativity: honest-by-design interface that puts the baseline and the negative result first, plus a plain-language "En clair" assistant.

Source code: Front end : https://github.com/Mrjojono/MeteoFront

Back end (FastAPI): https://github.com/Mrjojono/Nasa

Live API docs: https://pluie-prevue.fastapicloud.dev/docs
